Hard Hit Economy

By: Sophia Phirippides | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Is the cost of daily living exhausting your resources? Well, you are not alone. Carte Blanche’s exclusive economic report explains why spiraling debt is gripping the nation.

Unique Selling Point:
South African consumers have been hard hit in recent months and their future looks certain to get worse. A VAT increase in April, frequent fuel price hikes and rising electricity costs are taking their toll. Carte Blanche has an exclusive report, from economist Trinity Ncube, which reveals the knock on effects of these core increases. Earlier this year Carte Blanche forecast that people's buying power would decrease by 20%, but just three months later Trinity Ncube’s report shows that, in fact, consumers buying power has decreased by 25 to 30 percent. How are ordinary South African's coping with this extra burden on their pockets?

Summary:
Carte Blanche looks at the impact on markets and industries and the effects on struggling middle to higher income earners.

The rapid and record increases in fuel prices, the impending rise of municipality rates, together with the VAT hike, have combined to hit the real estate industry hard. Not to mention the barriers put up by the banks with their reluctance to provide bond opportunities for middle income earners.

So, housing sales are stagnant. To add to the economy’s woes, motorists are defaulting payments, risking repossessions and such luxuries as eating out have become unaffordable as consumers make cuts to their life style in a bid to make ends meet.

Economist Trinity Ncube suggests that central factors creating the current economic crisis are the weak Rand, the rising price of oil and the political climate engendered by policies such as Land Expropriation Without Compensation.

While the cost of living is rising inexorably, there has been little to no increase in income for the working class, particularly in the private sector. The outcome for consumers being, that they have lost about 25 to 30 percent in buying power.

When compiling the report, Trinity focused on middle income earners (ranging between an income of R16500 to R35000). Especially striking is the observation that for people earning the low middle income of about R16500, then the effect of the recent price escalation is to have pushed these earners back into a poverty income range.


Further information:
Carte Blanche speaks to the Estate Agents Affairs Board which regulates and monitors the real estate industry. The housing market has been impacted severely, especially for the middle to lower income groups. Houses for sale are not moving. Bongani from EAAB has cited Sydenham, in Johannesburg, as an illuminating example. There, about 43 houses have been on the market for the past six months and only about 3 have managed to sell. He says that a general change in demographics has also had a large impact on the industry. Such that, homeowners are now forced to sell their homes at very low prices or keep holding on to them, because they are not getting the prices they expect. Many upmarket areas like Witpoortjie on the West Rand, are no longer as “upmarket” as they once were. However, people who invested in the area, are unwilling to accept this fact. Carte Blanche speaks to the real estate agent who is tasked with selling houses in Sydenham and we will shoot homes on the market and the neighbourhoods that have been radically impacted.

According to the Motor Finance Corporation, there has been a high increase of clients defaulting on their car payments and having to reschedule their payment arrangements. Although repossession of vehicles is just at 1% nationally, due to the banks’ reluctance to repossess, the current trend shows a worrying trait of unaffordability. The losing battles, of individuals trying to pay for their vehicles, are signaled by a peak in the car auction industry. Nazeer from Gauteng Auctioneers in Johannesburg says that he has seen a high increase in the past year of repossessed vehicles that have ended up as lots in his showroom. Nazeer will take us through one of his auctions to visually indicate the number of vehicles that are being sold off. Trinity says that middle to lower income earners spend about 30% of their income on transport. With their decrease in buying power of 30%, this can be catastrophic to their household needs. The obvious short term solution is to let go of one’s precious car and revert to public transport. However, the solution is not as favourable as one would hope, because public transport fares have risen drastically over the past year due to the regular fuel hikes.

Sabelo Pitso, a single divorced mother has had to re-adjust her life to cope with the strains of the current economic climate. Earning a middle class salary of R20 000, she can no longer afford some of what she sees as basic essentials. She took out a R350 000 loan while she was in work. When Sabelo recently got retrenched, the bulk of her payout had to cover those debts. She cannot afford the schools she planned to take her two children to, with the aim of providing them with quality education. Now she worries that she is failing their future. Due to financial constraints, Sabelo has to say no to her children when it comes to extramural activities. In order to take her youngest child to a cheaper crèche, Sabelo has to spend extra money to drive the extra kilometres to get both her children to school. What Sabelo could comfortably afford in previous years is now almost impossible to pay for. Items such as clothing are a struggle and the situation is now so dire that Sabelo has resorted to dodging the taxman.

Dimi is a 35 year old single mother who runs her own business and also takes care of extended family members. She takes home a middle class income but it gets stretched so far that she cannot afford a car and even enough airtime and data to run her business. Due to the constant domestic responsibilities and rising cost of living, Dimi also opted to take out a loan - over R100 000 from African Bank that she now says that she has had to default on. She last paid an installment in March and spends her days dodging phone calls. Dimi regrets some of the financial decisions she has taken in the past as she sees them as the main contributing factors to her current predicament. She feels constantly tempted and pressurized by the repetitive messages on her phone, from banks, offering Dimi more of the same - more loans.

Bianca’s finances spiralled out of control in 2014. Her debts were way more than her income and that’s when she seeked debt review as a solution after a friend recommended it to her. She signed up with a debt review company but a year later her debts was not moving and had in fact increased. Bianca realized that her creditor was charging her insurance on her credit and her debt councilor was unaware of it. When she tried to get her debt councilor o help with the situation, they failed. Feeling anxious and depressed she then decided to seek advice from a Facebook friend who then suggested debt rescue, another debt councilor. Debt Rescue has managed to lower her monthly installments now and she is coping and following up with her current statements and all is going well. However Bianca now struggles with day-to-day costs of living, although she shares life with a domestic partner, they are financially constraint. Electricity and bills are high, transport and food is high and to top it all, she does not have kids of her own but her partner does so they have to use some of their income to help their kids in another household. Bianca has leaned some hard financial lesson and plans to be debts free by 2020 if all goes well with her debt councilor, but for now she has to suffer the consequences of her earlier financial mismanagement. Bianca is still ashamed of her financial situation and the only person who knows about it is her partner. She believes it would break her parents if they found out and for that reason she would like not to be identified on camera.

When consumers are hard hit and finding it difficult to cope they usually fall into spiraling debt and debt counseling may be their last resort. According to Charles Shonaye from Debt Sage, although the NCR has not released the latest numbers of consumers in debt, already about 8 million consumers are failing to pay or are defaulting on their payments. Numbers at Debt Sage do show that more and more consumers are opting for debt review and debt counseling.

The narrative will be framed around Trinity Ncube’s report, and we will highlight the key areas that will affect the middle class earners – housing, transport, food, utilities and managing debt.
Trinity will also give tips for how viewers can cut down on their expenses. We will ensure that we incorporate relevant visuals.

Press Release:


Hard hit by an increase in Vat, multiple fuel hikes and the soaring cost of basics like electricity, food and public transport, South African consumers have had their buying power slashed by 30%.

Script:


VO: It’s payback time for South Africans.

VO: With a 2.28 trillion rand national debt, the government’s severe tax remedies to tackle the country’s financial woes, are spreading hardship from the poor, to middle income earners.

VO: A new report by economist Trinity Ncube, explores the knock-on effect since April this year of the VAT increase, combined with multiple fuel and fuel levy hikes, inflated electricity costs, stealth taxes, and a weakening rand, that are depleting the purses of the people.

Trinity: From the first of April, up until now, everything has gone up: banking costs, transportation costs, anything that has value-added tax in it has increased we're looking at the ripple effect of all these things put together.

VO: Consumers, according to the report, are now likely to lose between 25 to 30% of their purchasing power.

Dimi: I wake up in the morning petrol has gone up, bread has gone up ETC….

VO: Dimi, a freelance filmmaker in the TV and Film industry earns on average R20 000 per month. As a single mom supporting an extended family, her earnings no longer cover her living costs.

Dimi: This year it doesn’t matter how much I discipline myself and say I’m going to the straight and narrow…...The 20 grand last year is a huge difference, it’s so little this year.

VO: Trinity has worked with over 3000 middle income earners in sustainable entrepreneurship over the past decade.

For his report he focused on middle income earners netting between R16500 and R25000 per month and interviewed more than 200 people

Trinity: We're looking at specific individuals, when they buy petrol how much they can buy per litre. When they're going to a shop, how much they can fill their basket

VO: Like most people in the report, David and Mary confess that in order to make their money stretch for essentials, there are some basic pleasures they now do without.

David: A braai. With a nice piece of steak. It's a no-no

Mary: There's no salads. There's pap

VO: Marcia, who runs her own business as an events organiser needs to look good for her clients

Marcia: When you've done a good event, you'd go out and get a pair of shoes to say, "Thank you. Well done, Marcia! You've done really good." But now there's no more thank yous. No more colognes. No more shoes. No more clothing.

Trinity: It is a very dangerous economic situation that we're in, From an income perspective, the middle-income earners,are starting to slide back into poverty.

VO: So if you are earning R20 000 a month, like Dimi, the net effect of losing 30% of your buying power means that in real terms you only have R14000 to spend, and that’s why Dimi’s budget is falling short.

Dimi: You know I had the dream that one day we should renovate… so I started building outside rooms, which is where we are currently staying with the whole family in one space.

VO: Dimi is fortunate to own a home even if her renovations are on hold, but for anyone wanting to buy a property, according to Clive Ashpol of the Estate Agency Affairs Board,
affordability is being stifled, especially in the lower to middle end of the market.

Clive: Those properties are not being sold and there are reasons for that, an inflated view of the value of the property on the part of the seller, resistance by purchasers and the fact that banks, in many cases, are not giving mortgage finance.

Trinity: So what we're saying here is there needs to be some transparency from the financial institutions as well as government in terms of regulations to say, "Why is it the case that you can give me a car loan and not a home loan?" Where the risks of the home loan are probably even less.

LINK: Often middle income earners qualify for loans and credit, but sometimes getting into debt is their only way to survive and maintain their lifestyle.

Dimi: You know those SMSs… what’s 40 grand, I can pay that… this girl is susceptible to accounts and she’s easy to take money

Trinity: Banks are not your friends. Banks are here to make money they do prey on people that are getting credit

VO: Before she knew it Dimi had racked up over R100k in loans including financing a car. But times got tougher and the creditors started calling.

Dimi: I kept dodging the phone calls, I found myself saying what do you want me to do, jump off a building?

Charles: If you're constantly getting calls from credit providers it's a sign that you really need help.

VO: Charles Shonayi, a debt counsellor, has seen a marked increase of people entering debt counselling over the last 6 months

Charles: Burying your head in the sand will be more trouble for you. I've seen many people coming to us when they are really in trouble and there is nothing that we can do. Whereas if they had sought help earlier then it's easy.

Trinity: from our study, we are finding one in every three persons has either missed a car payment or has missed a mortgage payment on their housing.

VO:David and Mary’s debt started piling up after Mary, who suffers from rheumatoid arthritis, had to give up her job. Suddenly their nuclear household of three was having to survive on David’s income of R18600 per month. Even though they put themselves into debt review they were unable to save their car.

Mary: We went into debt review with the finance house on the vehicle they didn’t respond to any requests, anything. The day the court order was issued, they issued summons and they came and took the car.

LINK: Even though banks say that repossession is their last resort, auction houses such as this one say they've seen a spike in repossessed vehicles on auction over the last six months.

sound up auction car selling… something about it being a steal…. would be in the cutaways bin

VO: Countrywide repossessions have increased by 1300 vehicles a month during the first six months of 2018, according to Trinity.

Marcia: OK, letting go of my car was a big thing for me. It was huge. It was even bigger than having--moving into a smaller place.

VO: Up until last year, the events business was good for Marcia. But when the work started slowing down she needed to give up something in order to feed her young family.

Marcia: it sort of like broke me. It broke my spirit a bit. So it is upsetting for me at the moment.

Mac: When did you start realising that you are not going to make it on a month-to-month basis?

Marcia: in June this year, it sort of like quietened it quietened down. You don't get as many requests as you would get of the personal birthday parties, the dinners, the baby showers. People just don't do that kind of thing any more. So there isn’t money for a good time.

VO: Even though Marcia is struggling, she believes debt counselling would be her last resort.

Marcia: I’m trying to remedy the situation on my own. I'm communicating to the people I owe What are my options?

VO: Going under Debt review can be taxing on an already stretched household budget. The Jacksons found, after paying the monthly R10 000 to service their debt, they’re left with only R8600 for everything else, including school fees, Mary’s excess medical bills, bond, transport, electricity and groceries

David: Basically we’ve got R700 for groceries, cleaning material dogfood, everything.

Mac: When was the last time you went on holiday?

Mary: Laugh, 2013

Mac: What are some of the things you’ve had to adjust drastically in your lifestyle?

David: I can’t remember when last I took my son just for a Steers burger… it just takes so much pride… out of you.

Marcia: I had cut down on most of the things. The children were going to a different school. That was like my biggest blow, to give me that awakening that it's bad. It told me it was really--now, it's rough.

Dimi:I haven’t bought clothes in how long, my hair thank god for these locks, I can do them myself, I haven’t coloured my hair, you see the blacks are coming out and the grey, now I’m exposed that I’m old.

Mac: Did you live beyond your means? did you want more than you should?

Marcia: What is expected from one’s family after education, the need to succeed for everyone, it puts a lot of pressure on one.

We put pressure on ourselves
Trinity: There's nothing wrong with wanting to live a better life. But live within your means. We have this competition. We have this posturing. So we don't look at the bigger picture. As a result we get into trouble.

VO: And the bigger picture is not looking rosy. Prices of goods and services continue to rise while salary increases have remained relatively stagnant between 3 to 6%. Middle income earners who stimulate growth in the economy may now be on the brink of poverty, and like David and Mary, they cling to what little they have left.

Jenny: The finance house said we should sell the house, pay their motor car, pay this house, and then where do we live? What do we do?

2018 Press Release: Hard hit by an increase in Vat, multiple fuel hikes and the soaring cost of basics like electricity, food and public transport, South African consumers have had their buying power slashed by 30%. Script: VO: It’s payback time for South Africans. VO: With a 2.28 trillion rand national debt, the government’s severe tax remedies to tackle the country’s financial woes, are spreading hardship from the poor, to middle income earners. VO: A new report by economist Trinity Ncube, explores the knock-on effect since April this year of the VAT increase, combined with multiple fuel and fuel levy hikes, inflated electricity costs, stealth taxes, and a weakening rand, that are depleting the purses of the people. Trinity: From the first of April, up until now, everything has gone up: banking costs, transportation costs, anything that has value-added tax in it has increased we're looking at the ripple effect of all these things put together. VO: Consumers, according to the report, are now likely to lose between 25 to 30% of their purchasing power. Dimi: I wake up in the morning petrol has gone up, bread has gone up ETC…. VO: Dimi, a freelance filmmaker in the TV and Film industry earns on average R20 000 per month. As a single mom supporting an extended family, her earnings no longer cover her living costs. Dimi: This year it doesn’t matter how much I discipline myself and say I’m going to the straight and narrow…...The 20 grand last year is a huge difference, it’s so little this year. VO: Trinity has worked with over 3000 middle income earners in sustainable entrepreneurship over the past decade. For his report he focused on middle income earners netting between R16500 and R25000 per month and interviewed more than 200 people Trinity: We're looking at specific individuals, when they buy petrol how much they can buy per litre. When they're going to a shop, how much they can fill their basket VO: Like most people in the report, David and Mary confess that in order to make their money stretch for essentials, there are some basic pleasures they now do without. David: A braai. With a nice piece of steak. It's a no-no Mary: There's no salads. There's pap VO: Marcia, who runs her own business as an events organiser needs to look good for her clients Marcia: When you've done a good event, you'd go out and get a pair of shoes to say, "Thank you. Well done, Marcia! You've done really good." But now there's no more thank yous. No more colognes. No more shoes. No more clothing. Trinity: It is a very dangerous economic situation that we're in, From an income perspective, the middle-income earners,are starting to slide back into poverty. VO: So if you are earning R20 000 a month, like Dimi, the net effect of losing 30% of your buying power means that in real terms you only have R14000 to spend, and that’s why Dimi’s budget is falling short. Dimi: You know I had the dream that one day we should renovate… so I started building outside rooms, which is where we are currently staying with the whole family in one space. VO: Dimi is fortunate to own a home even if her renovations are on hold, but for anyone wanting to buy a property, according to Clive Ashpol of the Estate Agency Affairs Board, affordability is being stifled, especially in the lower to middle end of the market. Clive: Those properties are not being sold and there are reasons for that, an inflated view of the value of the property on the part of the seller, resistance by purchasers and the fact that banks, in many cases, are not giving mortgage finance. Trinity: So what we're saying here is there needs to be some transparency from the financial institutions as well as government in terms of regulations to say, "Why is it the case that you can give me a car loan and not a home loan?" Where the risks of the home loan are probably even less. LINK: Often middle income earners qualify for loans and credit, but sometimes getting into debt is their only way to survive and maintain their lifestyle. Dimi: You know those SMSs… what’s 40 grand, I can pay that… this girl is susceptible to accounts and she’s easy to take money Trinity: Banks are not your friends. Banks are here to make money they do prey on people that are getting credit VO: Before she knew it Dimi had racked up over R100k in loans including financing a car. But times got tougher and the creditors started calling. Dimi: I kept dodging the phone calls, I found myself saying what do you want me to do, jump off a building? Charles: If you're constantly getting calls from credit providers it's a sign that you really need help. VO: Charles Shonayi, a debt counsellor, has seen a marked increase of people entering debt counselling over the last 6 months Charles: Burying your head in the sand will be more trouble for you. I've seen many people coming to us when they are really in trouble and there is nothing that we can do. Whereas if they had sought help earlier then it's easy. Trinity: from our study, we are finding one in every three persons has either missed a car payment or has missed a mortgage payment on their housing. VO:David and Mary’s debt started piling up after Mary, who suffers from rheumatoid arthritis, had to give up her job. Suddenly their nuclear household of three was having to survive on David’s income of R18600 per month. Even though they put themselves into debt review they were unable to save their car. Mary: We went into debt review with the finance house on the vehicle they didn’t respond to any requests, anything. The day the court order was issued, they issued summons and they came and took the car. LINK: Even though banks say that repossession is their last resort, auction houses such as this one say they've seen a spike in repossessed vehicles on auction over the last six months. sound up auction car selling… something about it being a steal…. would be in the cutaways bin VO: Countrywide repossessions have increased by 1300 vehicles a month during the first six months of 2018, according to Trinity. Marcia: OK, letting go of my car was a big thing for me. It was huge. It was even bigger than having--moving into a smaller place. VO: Up until last year, the events business was good for Marcia. But when the work started slowing down she needed to give up something in order to feed her young family. Marcia: it sort of like broke me. It broke my spirit a bit. So it is upsetting for me at the moment. Mac: When did you start realising that you are not going to make it on a month-to-month basis? Marcia: in June this year, it sort of like quietened it quietened down. You don't get as many requests as you would get of the personal birthday parties, the dinners, the baby showers. People just don't do that kind of thing any more. So there isn’t money for a good time. VO: Even though Marcia is struggling, she believes debt counselling would be her last resort. Marcia: I’m trying to remedy the situation on my own. I'm communicating to the people I owe What are my options? VO: Going under Debt review can be taxing on an already stretched household budget. The Jacksons found, after paying the monthly R10 000 to service their debt, they’re left with only R8600 for everything else, including school fees, Mary’s excess medical bills, bond, transport, electricity and groceries David: Basically we’ve got R700 for groceries, cleaning material dogfood, everything. Mac: When was the last time you went on holiday? Mary: Laugh, 2013 Mac: What are some of the things you’ve had to adjust drastically in your lifestyle? David: I can’t remember when last I took my son just for a Steers burger… it just takes so much pride… out of you. Marcia: I had cut down on most of the things. The children were going to a different school. That was like my biggest blow, to give me that awakening that it's bad. It told me it was really--now, it's rough. Dimi:I haven’t bought clothes in how long, my hair thank god for these locks, I can do them myself, I haven’t coloured my hair, you see the blacks are coming out and the grey, now I’m exposed that I’m old. Mac: Did you live beyond your means? did you want more than you should? Marcia: What is expected from one’s family after education, the need to succeed for everyone, it puts a lot of pressure on one. We put pressure on ourselves Trinity: There's nothing wrong with wanting to live a better life. But live within your means. We have this competition. We have this posturing. So we don't look at the bigger picture. As a result we get into trouble. VO: And the bigger picture is not looking rosy. Prices of goods and services continue to rise while salary increases have remained relatively stagnant between 3 to 6%. Middle income earners who stimulate growth in the economy may now be on the brink of poverty, and like David and Mary, they cling to what little they have left. Jenny: The finance house said we should sell the house, pay their motor car, pay this house, and then where do we live? What do we do?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Is the cost of daily living exhausting your resources? Well, you are not alone. Carte Blanche’s exclusive economic report explains why spiraling debt is gripping the nation.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: South African consumers have been hard hit in recent months and their future looks certain to get worse. A VAT increase in April, frequent fuel price hikes and rising electricity costs are taking their toll. Carte Blanche has an exclusive report, from economist Trinity Ncube, which reveals the knock on effects of these core increases. Earlier this year Carte Blanche forecast that people's buying power would decrease by 20%, but just three months later Trinity Ncube’s report shows that, in fact, consumers buying power has decreased by 25 to 30 percent. How are ordinary South African's coping with this extra burden on their pockets?
metadata.Summary: Carte Blanche looks at the impact on markets and industries and the effects on struggling middle to higher income earners. The rapid and record increases in fuel prices, the impending rise of municipality rates, together with the VAT hike, have combined to hit the real estate industry hard. Not to mention the barriers put up by the banks with their reluctance to provide bond opportunities for middle income earners. So, housing sales are stagnant. To add to the economy’s woes, motorists are defaulting payments, risking repossessions and such luxuries as eating out have become unaffordable as consumers make cuts to their life style in a bid to make ends meet. Economist Trinity Ncube suggests that central factors creating the current economic crisis are the weak Rand, the rising price of oil and the political climate engendered by policies such as Land Expropriation Without Compensation. While the cost of living is rising inexorably, there has been little to no increase in income for the working class, particularly in the private sector. The outcome for consumers being, that they have lost about 25 to 30 percent in buying power. When compiling the report, Trinity focused on middle income earners (ranging between an income of R16500 to R35000). Especially striking is the observation that for people earning the low middle income of about R16500, then the effect of the recent price escalation is to have pushed these earners back into a poverty income range.
metadata.Further information: Carte Blanche speaks to the Estate Agents Affairs Board which regulates and monitors the real estate industry. The housing market has been impacted severely, especially for the middle to lower income groups. Houses for sale are not moving. Bongani from EAAB has cited Sydenham, in Johannesburg, as an illuminating example. There, about 43 houses have been on the market for the past six months and only about 3 have managed to sell. He says that a general change in demographics has also had a large impact on the industry. Such that, homeowners are now forced to sell their homes at very low prices or keep holding on to them, because they are not getting the prices they expect. Many upmarket areas like Witpoortjie on the West Rand, are no longer as “upmarket” as they once were. However, people who invested in the area, are unwilling to accept this fact. Carte Blanche speaks to the real estate agent who is tasked with selling houses in Sydenham and we will shoot homes on the market and the neighbourhoods that have been radically impacted. According to the Motor Finance Corporation, there has been a high increase of clients defaulting on their car payments and having to reschedule their payment arrangements. Although repossession of vehicles is just at 1% nationally, due to the banks’ reluctance to repossess, the current trend shows a worrying trait of unaffordability. The losing battles, of individuals trying to pay for their vehicles, are signaled by a peak in the car auction industry. Nazeer from Gauteng Auctioneers in Johannesburg says that he has seen a high increase in the past year of repossessed vehicles that have ended up as lots in his showroom. Nazeer will take us through one of his auctions to visually indicate the number of vehicles that are being sold off. Trinity says that middle to lower income earners spend about 30% of their income on transport. With their decrease in buying power of 30%, this can be catastrophic to their household needs. The obvious short term solution is to let go of one’s precious car and revert to public transport. However, the solution is not as favourable as one would hope, because public transport fares have risen drastically over the past year due to the regular fuel hikes. Sabelo Pitso, a single divorced mother has had to re-adjust her life to cope with the strains of the current economic climate. Earning a middle class salary of R20 000, she can no longer afford some of what she sees as basic essentials. She took out a R350 000 loan while she was in work. When Sabelo recently got retrenched, the bulk of her payout had to cover those debts. She cannot afford the schools she planned to take her two children to, with the aim of providing them with quality education. Now she worries that she is failing their future. Due to financial constraints, Sabelo has to say no to her children when it comes to extramural activities. In order to take her youngest child to a cheaper crèche, Sabelo has to spend extra money to drive the extra kilometres to get both her children to school. What Sabelo could comfortably afford in previous years is now almost impossible to pay for. Items such as clothing are a struggle and the situation is now so dire that Sabelo has resorted to dodging the taxman. Dimi is a 35 year old single mother who runs her own business and also takes care of extended family members. She takes home a middle class income but it gets stretched so far that she cannot afford a car and even enough airtime and data to run her business. Due to the constant domestic responsibilities and rising cost of living, Dimi also opted to take out a loan - over R100 000 from African Bank that she now says that she has had to default on. She last paid an installment in March and spends her days dodging phone calls. Dimi regrets some of the financial decisions she has taken in the past as she sees them as the main contributing factors to her current predicament. She feels constantly tempted and pressurized by the repetitive messages on her phone, from banks, offering Dimi more of the same - more loans. Bianca’s finances spiralled out of control in 2014. Her debts were way more than her income and that’s when she seeked debt review as a solution after a friend recommended it to her. She signed up with a debt review company but a year later her debts was not moving and had in fact increased. Bianca realized that her creditor was charging her insurance on her credit and her debt councilor was unaware of it. When she tried to get her debt councilor o help with the situation, they failed. Feeling anxious and depressed she then decided to seek advice from a Facebook friend who then suggested debt rescue, another debt councilor. Debt Rescue has managed to lower her monthly installments now and she is coping and following up with her current statements and all is going well. However Bianca now struggles with day-to-day costs of living, although she shares life with a domestic partner, they are financially constraint. Electricity and bills are high, transport and food is high and to top it all, she does not have kids of her own but her partner does so they have to use some of their income to help their kids in another household. Bianca has leaned some hard financial lesson and plans to be debts free by 2020 if all goes well with her debt councilor, but for now she has to suffer the consequences of her earlier financial mismanagement. Bianca is still ashamed of her financial situation and the only person who knows about it is her partner. She believes it would break her parents if they found out and for that reason she would like not to be identified on camera. When consumers are hard hit and finding it difficult to cope they usually fall into spiraling debt and debt counseling may be their last resort. According to Charles Shonaye from Debt Sage, although the NCR has not released the latest numbers of consumers in debt, already about 8 million consumers are failing to pay or are defaulting on their payments. Numbers at Debt Sage do show that more and more consumers are opting for debt review and debt counseling. The narrative will be framed around Trinity Ncube’s report, and we will highlight the key areas that will affect the middle class earners – housing, transport, food, utilities and managing debt. Trinity will also give tips for how viewers can cut down on their expenses. We will ensure that we incorporate relevant visuals.
